Issued at 227 PM CDT Sat Aug 8 2026

A surface high is settling into the northern Mississippi Valley
and western Great Lakes this afternoon in the wake of the this 
morning's cold front. Despite the northwest winds and the hazy 
skies, temperatures have still managed to warm into the lower 
80s and should be able to warm another 2-3 degrees prior to 
sunset. Winds will turn more southeasterly overnight as the 
surface high slides overhead with temperatures cooling into the 
lower to mid-60s. 

While we enjoy a quiet summer night tonight, a shortwave trough
will be ejecting across the northern Plains. This shortwave is 
expected to lead to the development of a cluster of 
thunderstorms across SD and MN overnight that will gradually 
west-southwest with time. There is also a chance for some 
scattered showers and storms to develop on the nose of the low-
level jet in IA and MO tonight, but guidance has been 
inconsistent with coverage of storms there so confidence on that
occurring is low. Regardless of what develops in IA/MO tonight,
the northern complex is expected to ride the instability 
gradient and drift towards northern IL. Initially it looked as 
if the better instability would remain south and west of our 
area which in turn would keep storms outside of our area through
Sunday morning. However, recent trends now show last night's 
front lifting back north as a warm front overnight into Sunday 
morning which looks to bring the better instability axis into 
our area prior to the complex arriving. Therefore, confidence is
increasing that a complex of thunderstorms will move across 
northern IL and northwest IN during the morning hours on Sunday.
Since the storms are forecast to arrive prior to the atmosphere
fully destabilizing, the expectation is for the storms to move 
through in a decaying state. As a result, confidence in storm 
coverage with eastward extent is lower but the thinking is at 
least some isolated to scattered storms will traverse across 
most of the area between 9 AM and 12 PM CDT. Given the decaying 
nature of the storms, the severe threat in the morning looks low
at this time but instances of gusty winds and hail could occur 
with the strongest storms. 

Heading into Sunday afternoon, the aforementioned warm front 
should be stalled across northern IL and northwest IN which will
serve as the focus for a second round of thunderstorms Sunday 
afternoon and evening as another shortwave pivots through. While
confidence on the second round of storms occurring is fairly 
high (70-80% chance of occurrence), confidence is lower in the 
exact time storms will redevelop and where the greatest coverage
will be. The reason is because the morning round of storms 
could limit how quickly the atmosphere destabilizes and thus 
delay the redevelopment of storms until later in the afternoon 
or even the evening. Regardless of when and where storms 
initialize, the environment in place Sunday afternoon and 
evening will be very unstable (MLCAPE values around 3000-5000 
J/kg) with 35-45 kts of deep layer shear which will support 
thunderstorms organizing and becoming severe. The main severe 
threat with the storms will be damaging winds upwards of 60+ 
mph, but instances of hail and perhaps a tornado or two cannot 
be ruled out given the steep mid-level lapse rates and veering 
low-level wind field respectively. Due to this threat the Storm
Prediction Center has maintained the slight risk (level 2 of 5)
across our entire forecast area. 

In addition to the severe weather threat, there is also a 
conditional threat for flash flooding to materialize given the 
humid air mass (PWATs around 2 inches) and favorable storm 
parameters. The condition, though, is whether or not storms 
train over the same locations Sunday afternoon/evening or if 
they remain transient enough to limit the heavy rainfall in any 
one location. With the aforementioned uncertainties in storm 
coverage Sunday afternoon/evening, confidence is too low to 
warrant the issuance of a Flood Watch at this time but something
we will be monitoring as the event unfolds. Furthermore, there 
is also the potential for storms to keep festering overnight 
Sunday night as the low-level jet ramps up in the proximity of 
the stalled frontal boundary. If coverage of storms Sunday night
is more expansive, then the threat for flash flooding could 
quickly increase especially if coverage of afternoon/evening 
storms is higher. That said, there is a chance (20-30%) for a 
swath of 2-3+ inch rain amounts to occur somewhere in our 
forecast area so remain on guard particularly if you live in an 
urban or lower-lying area.
